2,3-Allenoic acids via palladium-catalyzed carboxylation of 
propargylic alcohols 
Wei-Feng Zheng,a Wanli Zhang,c Jianhao Huang,d Yibo Yu,d Hui Qian,*a Shengming Ma*a,b 
A straightforward protocol for the synthesis of tetra-substituted 2,3-allenoic acids via a catalytic carboxylation of the 
readily available propargylic alcohols in the presence of CO using palladium and Brønsted acid as the cocatalysts has been 
established. This atom-economic reaction proceeded under mild conditions to afford 2,3-allenoic acids with a broad scope 
tolerating useful functional groups. 
Introduction 
Allenes are not only a common structural motif in natural 
products, biologically active compounds, 1 and advanced 
materials,2 but also serve as attractive precursors in a variety 
of organic transformations.3 Among functionalized allenes, 2,3-
allenoic acids are of great interest since they may be readily 
transformed into allenols (then, amines, halides, or tosylates, 
etc.),4 allenals, 5 allenoates, 6 allenamides, 7 and butenolides. 8 
Thus, the development of efficient methods for the synthesis 
of these compounds is of great interest. Traditional approach 
to 2,3-allenoic acids is the hydrolysis of 2,3-allenoates, which 
usually yielded a mixture of allenoic acids and alkynoic 
acids.
9,10 Carboxylation reaction of allenylmetallic reagents 
with carbon dioxide, 11 the oxidation of allenols, 12 and the 
isomerization of but-3-ynoic acid and 4-(trimethylsilyl)but-3-
ynoic acid were also reported,
11d,13 but these methods suffer 
from poor atom- or step-economy, harsh reaction conditions, 
or limited substrate scope. It is believed that the carboxylation 
of the readily available propargylic alcohols or their derivatives 
such as carbonates, acetates, etc. with CO in the presence of 
water should be the most atom economic way for synthesis of 
allenoic acids. The reports on such a strategy are very limited 
although the related carbonylations of the related propargylic 
derivatives affording the allenoates are well established. 10 The 
challenge should be the poor nucleophilicity of water. Nickel- 
or palladium-catalyzed carboxylations of propargylic halides or 
mesylates were reported to afford a mixture of 2,3-allenoic 
acids and itaconic acids (Scheme 1a).
10c,14 In 1994, Inoue and 
co-workers developed the Pd-catalyzed carboxylation of 2-
methyl-3-alkynols affording a mixture of 2,3-allenoic acids and 
2(5H)-furanones with a high pressure of CO (10 atm) (Scheme 
1b).
15 It should also be noted that the reaction of propargylic 
alcohol in the presence of a transition metal catalyst and 
carbon monoxide afforded lactones.
15,16 Previously, we 
reported the alkoxycarbonylation of propargylic alcohols 
(Scheme 1c).
10l Here, we report the first example on 
palladium-catalyzed carboxylation of propargylic alcohols with 
a catalytic phosphoric acid as the cocatalyst to afford tetra-
substituted 2,3-allenoic acids exclusively. 
 
Scheme 1. Transition metal-catalyzed carboxylation approaches toward 2,3-allenoic 
acids 
Results and discussion 
Our investigations commenced with the Pd/H +-cocatalyzed 
reaction of 2-phenyloct-3-yn-2-ol ( 1a) as model substrate. In 
the presence of [PdCl(π-allyl)] 2, DPEphos, (PhO) 2POOH, and

H2O in toluene with CO (provided by a balloon), the reaction 
furnished the expected 2,3-allenoic acid 2a in 62% yield, albeit 
together with 4% yield of 2,4-alkadienoic acid 3a17 (Table 1, 
entry 1).10l It was noted that the yield was much lower with 
Xantphos as the ligand (Table 1, entry 2). When BIPHEP was 
employed, a mixture of allenoic acid 2a, 2,4-dienoic acid  3a, 
and enyne 4a were obtained with a poor selectivity (Table 1, 
entry 3). When PPh 3 was employed, this reaction afforded the 
dehydration product enyne 4a as the major product (Table 1, 
entry 4). Zheda-phos 18 exhibited no catalytic activity (Table 1, 
entry 5). Catalyst screening was conducted with DPEphos as 
the ligand: No expected product was formed with Pd(PPh
3)4 or 
Pd2(dba)3·CHCl3. Interestingly, it turned out that PdCl 2 is the 
best (Table 1, entries 6, 7, and 8). The efficiency was reduced 
when the amount of water was decreased to 4 equiv (Table 1, 
entry 9). Very limited level of reaction was observed in the 
absence of water (Table 1, entry 10). Thus, optimal results 
were defined as 2 mol% of PdCl
2, 6 mol% DPEphos, 5 mol% 
(PhO)2POOH, and 8.0 equiv of H 2O in toluene at 50 oC under 1 
atm of CO (Table 1, entry 8) affording the desired allenoic acid 
product in 97% NMR yield. 
Table 1. Optimization of the reaction conditions for the carboxylation of 1a a 
 
With the optimal reaction conditions in hand, the scope of 
the method was examined. As shown in Table 2, a variety of 
tertiary propargylic alcohols bearing differently substituted 
phenyl group (R 1) were initially surveyed. The substrates with 
electron-donating and electron-withdrawing group substituted 
aryl group could be employed in our protocol (
2a-2f). There is 
no obvious influence on the steric effect since substrates 
bearing the methyl group at the o-, m-, and p-position of the 
phenyl group all afford the desired products with high yields 
(2b-2d). The C-Br bond survived affording 2f. R1 may also be an 
alkyl group (entry 17). The reaction of 2-(naphth-2-yl)oct-3-yn-
2-ol delivered 2g in 93% yield. When R1 is a phenyl ring, R2 may 
vary from alkyl to phenyl group giving the carboxylation 
products 
2h-2j in 53-97% yields. Next, we turned our attention 
to the scope of the R 3 group: alkyl group such as n-propyl, n-
hexyl, i-propyl, chloropropyl and phenyl may all work to afford 
the corresponding products in good to excellent yields ( 2k-2p). 
The structure of 2p was confirmed by single-crystal X-ray 
diffraction analysis (Figure 1). 19 In addition, all alkyl 
substitution propargylic alcohol 1q was also amenable to 
carboxylation to afford 2q in 56% yield.

Gram-scale reaction of 1o afforded carboxylated product 
2o in 92% yield under the standard conditions (eq. 1). 
 
The synthetic application of product 2o is demonstrated in 
Scheme 2: When 2o was treated with CuCl, the 
cycloisomerization product 2(5 H)-furanone 5 was obtained in 
93% yield. 20 4-Bromo-2(5 H)-furanone 6 was obtained in 
excellent yield via a bromolactonization reaction. This 2,3-
allenoic acid 2o may also undergo a fluorolactonization 
reaction with Selectfluor to afford 7 in 73% yield. 21 A 
palladium-catalyzed cyclization-allylation reaction of 2o in the 
presence of allyl bromide furnished allylated butenolide 8 with 
79% yield.8g 
Scheme 2. Cyclization reactions 2,3-allenoic acid 2o 
To gain further insight into the mechanism, we carried out 
some control experiments. Firstly, no reaction occurred 
without the addition of (PhO)
2PO2H (eq. 2). We hypothesize 
the phosphate 9 may be formed in situ as the reactive species. 
Thus, we mixed 1a with 1 equiv. (PhO) 2PO2H at 50 oC, 
however, the formation of 9 was not observed (eq. 3), instead, 
the dehydration product enyne 4a was formed. When enyne 
4a was submitted to the standard conditions, only trace 
amount of 2a was detected, which suggests the enyne is not 
the possible intermediate (eq. 4). The hydroxy group in the 
carboxyl unit of the allenoic acids may come from the hydroxy 
group in the propargylic alcohols, however, the reaction rate 
was very slow in the absence of water (eq. 5), which suggested 
the hydroxy group mostly came from the added water. 
 
A possible catalytic cycle for this Pd/H + co-catalyzed 
carboxylation reaction was proposed (Scheme 3). At the 
beginning, Brønsted acid activated propargylic alcohol to 
generate the oxonium intermediate I, which would undergo 
oxidative addition with Pd(0) to produce the key 
allenylpalladium intermediate II. The allenylpalladium species 
would react with CO and H 2O to give intermediate III and/or 
IV. Subsequent reductive elimination would furnish the 
products and regenerate the palladium(0) catalyst. 
Scheme 3. A proposed catalytic cycle 
Conclusions 
In summary, we have developed a straightforward protocol 
for the synthesis of tetra-substituted 2,3-allenoic acids via a 
catalytic carboxylation of the readily available propargylic 
alcohols in the presence of CO using palladium and Brønsted 
acid as the cocatalysts. The reaction proceeded in an atom-
economical way under mild conditions. Further studies related 
to this topic are currently ongoing in our laboratory. 
Conflicts of interest 
There are no conflicts to declare.
